title: Node.js in production — variant 3
description: Capacity math and caching, the DNS-threadpool trap, load shedding, container CPU sizing, warm-up and readiness, GC near the heap limit, object-mode buffers, retry storms and ESM tracing.

questions.stem: A fashion retailer server-renders product pages in Node: about 80 ms of CPU per page. A flash sale will bring 1 200 rps to 40 hot products, and prices and stock badges may be up to 10 seconds stale. Which plan handles the sale at the lowest cost?

options.text: Move rendering into a worker-thread pool on every pod.
options.why: It keeps the loops responsive, but 1 200 × 80 ms still needs about 96 cores of rendering, which is what you were trying to avoid.

options.text: Cache each rendered page per product for 10 s and render on a miss.
options.why: With 40 hot products and a 10 s TTL, renders drop to about 4 per second; the loop serves cached HTML in microseconds.

options.text: Scale out to about 100 pods for the sale window, then scale back in afterwards.
options.why: It works but costs about 100 cores to re-render the same 40 pages thousands of times a second.

options.text: Chunk the render with `setImmediate` so requests interleave.
options.why: Interleaving spreads the CPU but doesn't reduce it; the pods saturate and every page gets slower.

questions.explain: Capacity math first: CPU per request × rps = cores needed. When many requests produce identical output and some staleness is allowed, a short-TTL cache removes the work entirely, which beats any way of parallelising it.

questions.stem: A marketplace API validates request bodies with Ajv. To support per-tenant schemas, a developer moved `ajv.compile(schema)` into the request handler. After the release, p50 latency went from 8 ms to 45 ms and the pods' CPU doubled, though traffic is unchanged and there are only 30 tenant schemas. Which fix is right?

options.text: Compile once per schema and reuse the validator.
options.why: Compiling generates code and is CPU-heavy; with 30 schemas, a cache of compiled validators makes the per-request cost a lookup.

options.text: Move validation into a worker-thread pool so the main loop stays free.
options.why: It relieves the main loop but keeps doing the same compilation per request, now plus a clone of every body.

options.text: Switch to a faster validator library.
options.why: A faster compiler shrinks each compile but still compiles on every request; the waste stays in the hot path.

options.text: Add pods to absorb the extra CPU.
options.why: You pay permanently for repeated, avoidable work.

questions.explain: Anything that compiles (schemas, regexes, templates, prepared queries) belongs at start-up or in a bounded cache, never on the per-request path. A latency jump with flat traffic after a refactor usually means work moved into the hot path.

questions.stem: A webhook dispatcher POSTs events to 5 000 different customer hostnames. Some customers' DNS servers take 5 s to answer. When those hosts get events, the dispatcher's unrelated `fs` writes and async `crypto` signing slow to seconds, while event-loop delay stays low. Which change addresses the cause?

options.text: Increase the HTTP agent's `maxSockets` so more requests run in parallel.
options.why: More parallel requests mean more parallel slow lookups, which fill the shared pool faster.

options.text: Lower the fetch timeout to 1 s.
options.why: The timeout abandons the request, but the `getaddrinfo` call keeps its threadpool thread until DNS answers.

options.text: Cache DNS results and resolve with `dns.resolve*` (c-ares) instead of the threadpool-based `dns.lookup`.
options.why: `dns.lookup` uses `getaddrinfo` on libuv's 4-thread pool, so slow DNS blocks fs and crypto behind it. A cache plus the c-ares resolver keeps lookups off the pool.

options.text: Move signing to `crypto.signSync` so it skips the queue.
options.why: Synchronous signing blocks the event loop for every request, which is worse.

questions.explain: `dns.lookup` (the default for `http` and `net`) is not network I/O on the loop; it is a blocking `getaddrinfo` call on libuv's threadpool, shared with fs, crypto and zlib. Slow DNS can starve unrelated work. Cache lookups and size the pool deliberately.

questions.stem: During a ticket on-sale, a Node API received three times its capacity. Event-loop delay reached 8 s, every request took longer than the clients' 5 s timeout, the clients retried, and goodput fell to almost zero although the pods were 100% busy. Autoscaling needs 3 minutes. Which change keeps the service useful during the next spike?

options.text: Raise the server's `requestTimeout` so slow requests complete.
options.why: Completed responses arrive after clients have given up and retried, so the CPU still goes to work nobody receives.

options.text: Shed load: 503 + `Retry-After` when loop delay passes a threshold.
options.why: Rejecting excess work cheaply keeps latency low for admitted requests, so the capacity you have produces useful responses while autoscaling catches up.

options.text: Queue every request in an in-memory FIFO until a worker slot frees up.
options.why: An unbounded queue only adds latency and memory; queued requests time out on the client side anyway.

options.text: Lower the HPA target so it reacts earlier.
options.why: It helps the next ramp slightly, but a 3-minute scale-up still leaves the overload window unprotected.

questions.explain: Overload causes congestion collapse: everything is served late and wasted. Measure the loop (delay or ELU) and reject early and cheaply above a threshold so admitted requests stay fast; retries need backoff and `Retry-After`.

questions.stem: An e-mail rendering service calls `fs.readFileSync(templatePath)` on each request because a `cacheTemplates: false` flag from development leaked into production. Templates sit on an EFS volume. At 400 rps, p99 jumps to seconds whenever EFS latency rises, for all endpoints, not just e-mail. Which fix is best?

options.text: Switch to `await fs.promises.readFile` on each request so the loop never blocks.
options.why: It stops blocking the loop, but it still does 400 network-file reads per second and queues them on the 4-thread libuv pool.

options.text: Move the templates to the container image's local disk.
options.why: Local disk is faster, but synchronous reads per request still block the loop under load, and template updates now need a redeploy.

options.text: Load templates once at start-up, or cache them, and render from memory.
options.why: Templates rarely change, so reading them per request is pure waste; from memory there is no blocking and no EFS dependency on the hot path.

options.text: Increase the pod count until p99 recovers.
options.why: Every pod still blocks on EFS; more pods just add more readers.

questions.explain: Synchronous I/O in a request handler blocks every request on the process, and its cost is set by the slowest storage involved. Read static assets at start-up or cache them; keep sync calls out of request paths.

questions.stem: A grocery app keeps shopping carts in a `Map` inside each Node process and uses ALB sticky sessions. Every scale-in and every deploy empties some customers' carts, and conversion dropped 3% on deploy days. Which change fits?

options.text: Raise the sticky-session cookie duration to 7 days.
options.why: Stickiness doesn't help when the pod itself goes away, which is exactly what scale-in and deploys do.

options.text: Disable scale-in and deploy only at night.
options.why: It reduces how often carts are lost, and costs both capacity efficiency and delivery speed.

options.text: Keep carts in Redis or the database with a TTL.
options.why: With carts in a shared store, pods become disposable: scale-in, crashes and deploys no longer lose customer state, and stickiness becomes unnecessary.

options.text: Write the cart map to the pod's disk on SIGTERM.
options.why: The disk goes away with the pod, and SIGTERM handling doesn't cover crashes or OOM kills.

questions.explain: Replicas must be disposable. User state that must outlive a process (sessions, carts, uploads in progress) belongs in a shared store; sticky sessions are a crutch that fails on exactly the events autoscaling causes.

questions.stem: A video-thumbnail service sizes its `worker_threads` pool with `os.cpus().length`. Pods have a 2-CPU limit and run on 32-core nodes. Latency is erratic, and metrics show heavy CFS throttling. Which change fits?

options.text: Size the pool from the pod's CPU limit (passed in as config), leaving a core for the main loop.
options.why: `os.cpus()` reports the host's cores, so the pool starts 32 threads against a 2-CPU quota; sizing from the limit stops the quota being burned in bursts and throttled.

options.text: Remove the CPU limit so the pool can use the whole node.
options.why: Throttling stops, but the pod now competes with every other workload on the node, and its cost and behaviour depend on its neighbours.

options.text: Raise `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` to 32 to match.
options.why: That is libuv's pool for native async work, not the worker-thread pool, and more threads make throttling worse.

options.text: Use the `cluster` module instead of worker threads.
options.why: Forking a process per reported CPU has the same miscount, plus duplicated memory.

questions.explain: Inside containers, `os.cpus()` shows the host, not your quota. Size thread and process pools from the CPU limit you set; too many busy threads against a small quota cause throttling and latency spikes rather than throughput.

questions.stem: A SaaS API runs both HTTP handlers and a BullMQ job processor (PDF generation, CSV imports) in the same pods. When a customer imports a 2 GB CSV, API p99 goes from 60 ms to 2 s on whichever pods pick up the import jobs. Which change fits?

options.text: Set the BullMQ job concurrency to 1 on each pod.
options.why: It limits jobs per pod, but one heavy import still shares the loop and CPU with the API on that pod.

options.text: A separate job-processor deployment, scaled on queue depth.
options.why: API and batch work stop competing for one loop, and each side scales on its own signal: request latency for the API, backlog for the workers.

options.text: Give the API pods more CPU.
options.why: Extra CPU doesn't help the single JS loop that the import is blocking.

options.text: Lower the import job's priority so API-adjacent jobs are processed first.
options.why: Priority orders jobs against each other; once an import runs, it still competes with the API on that pod.

questions.explain: Separate latency-sensitive serving from throughput-oriented batch work at the deployment level. Each gets its own scaling signal and failure domain, and a heavy job can't steal the event loop from user requests.

questions.stem: A travel search API loads a 1.2 GB fare table into memory at start-up, which takes about 90 s. During a traffic spike the HPA added 20 pods, which passed readiness after 5 s and returned 500s for over a minute because the table wasn't loaded. Which change fixes the scale-out?

options.text: Make readiness (or a startup probe) succeed only after the fare table has loaded.
options.why: Pods then receive traffic only once they can serve it; the load balancer keeps using warm pods until the new ones are ready.

options.text: Increase `initialDelaySeconds` on readiness to 120 s.
options.why: It works when loading takes under 120 s, but it's a guess: slower loads still fail, and faster ones wait for nothing.

options.text: Return 503 from handlers until the table is loaded.
options.why: Better than 500, but the load balancer still routes to the pod, and clients get errors for a minute.

options.text: Load the table lazily on the first request.
options.why: The first requests then wait 90 s or fail, and many concurrent first requests can trigger parallel loads.

questions.explain: Readiness should mean "can serve correctly now", tied to the actual warm-up state rather than a timer. Slow warm-up also sets how fast you can scale out, so pre-scale or shrink the warm-up for spiky traffic.

questions.stem: A pricing engine legitimately keeps about 1.1 GB of live data in memory. Years ago it ran in 1.5 GiB pods with `--max-old-space-size=1280`; pods are now 4 GiB, but the flag was never changed. Latency spikes every few seconds, and GC traces show back-to-back mark-compacts that free little. Which change fits?

options.text: Call `global.gc()` every second so collection happens in small, predictable steps.
options.why: The live data is genuinely needed; forced GCs find nothing to free and add pauses.

options.text: Move the data into a worker thread.
options.why: The worker has its own heap, which needs the same size; it moves the GC thrash rather than fixing it.

options.text: Raise `--max-old-space-size` to ~3 GB, under the 4 GiB limit.
options.why: The heap is nearly full of live data, so V8 keeps collecting to stay under the old cap; room above the live set makes major GCs rare.

options.text: Lower `--max-semi-space-size` to shorten young-generation pauses.
options.why: The problem is old-space mark-compacts near the heap cap, not scavenges.

questions.explain: When the live set approaches the heap limit, V8 runs major GCs back to back and frees little: latency suffers long before the OOM. Size the heap to the live set plus headroom, and keep the flag in step with the container limit.

questions.stem: A medical-imaging pipeline is a four-stage `pipeline` of object-mode Transforms. Each object carries a 5 MB scan. Memory per pipeline peaks around 300 MB, and the pod can run only a few pipelines in parallel. The byte-mode streams elsewhere use a 64 KiB high-water mark. Which change bounds memory most directly?

options.text: Set `highWaterMark: 1` (or 2) on the object-mode stages.
options.why: In object mode the high-water mark counts objects, defaulting to 16; with 5 MB objects, each stage can buffer about 80 MB. A small count bounds the buffer in bytes.

options.text: Set `highWaterMark: 65536` on those stages to match the byte-mode streams.
options.why: In object mode that means 65 536 objects, which effectively removes backpressure.

options.text: Switch from `pipeline` to `.pipe()`.
options.why: Same buffering, but you lose error propagation and cleanup.

options.text: Lower the pod's heap limit so GC runs more often.
options.why: Buffered objects are referenced, so GC cannot free them; it just crashes sooner.

questions.explain: Object-mode streams measure buffers in objects, not bytes (default 16). When objects are large, set the high-water mark explicitly, because buffer memory is about stages × high-water mark × object size.

questions.stem: A public bulk-import endpoint reads its body with `const data = await json(req)` from `node:stream/consumers`. Someone sent a 2 GB body. The pod spent 40 s reading it, then crashed with an out-of-memory error, taking 300 other requests with it. Which change fits?

options.text: Increase the heap limit to 4 GB.
options.why: It survives this body and fails on a bigger one; one client still controls your memory.

options.text: Wrap `json(req)` in `try/catch`.
options.why: An out-of-memory crash isn't a catchable exception, and parsing a huge body also blocks the loop.

options.text: Enforce a body size limit (`Content-Length` check plus a byte counter that aborts), and stream large imports.
options.why: Rejecting oversized bodies early bounds memory per request, and streaming parsing handles legitimate large imports without holding them whole.

options.text: Rate-limit the endpoint to 1 request per minute per client.
options.why: A single request is enough to crash the pod, so rate limiting doesn't bound memory.

questions.explain: Every consumer that collects a whole stream (`json()`, `text()`, `arrayBuffer()`) needs a size bound when the input is untrusted. Count bytes as they arrive and abort past the limit; stream anything legitimately large.

questions.stem: A request passes through three Node services: BFF → Orders → Payments. Each calls the next with a 2 s timeout and 3 retries. During a 1-minute Payments slowdown, Payments' request rate rose to roughly 27 times normal and it fell over completely. Which change prevents this?

options.text: Keep the retries but use exponential backoff with full jitter at every layer.
options.why: Jitter spreads the retries out in time, but the 3 × 3 × 3 multiplication of attempts remains.

options.text: Raise each timeout to 10 s so fewer requests time out.
options.why: Fewer timeouts, but slow calls hold sockets and memory longer at every hop, and callers above give up anyway.

options.text: Retry at one layer, within a retry budget, and pass the deadline down.
options.why: Retries multiply across layers; one retrying layer with a budget (for example 10% of requests) bounds the amplification, and deadlines stop work past the caller's timeout.

options.text: Add more Payments replicas.
options.why: Its load is 27× normal; adding capacity for a retry storm is expensive and still loses to the multiplier.

questions.explain: Retries at every hop multiply: n layers with r attempts each give r^n calls on the deepest service. Retry in one place, cap retries with a budget, use jittered backoff, and propagate deadlines so no one retries for a caller who has gone.

questions.stem: A crawler service passes an app-wide `shutdownSignal` into every page fetch, using the helper shown. After a few hours the logs fill with `MaxListenersExceededWarning`, and heap snapshots show millions of closures retained by the signal. Which fix is right?

options.text: Raise the listener limit with `events.setMaxListeners(Infinity, shutdownSignal)`.
options.why: It silences the warning; the listeners and the closures they retain still pile up.

options.text: Create a new controller per fetch and never abort on shutdown.
options.why: It removes the leak by dropping shutdown cancellation, so in-flight fetches block the shutdown.

options.text: Abort the shutdown signal every hour and create a new one.
options.why: That cancels all in-flight work every hour to clear listeners.

options.text: Remove the listener when the fetch ends, for example with `using` and `events.addAbortListener()`.
options.why: `addAbortListener` returns a Disposable, so `using` (or a `finally` that disposes it) removes the listener when each operation finishes.

questions.explain: Long-lived signals collect a listener for every operation that subscribes. Always unsubscribe when the operation ends; `events.addAbortListener` with `using` makes that automatic. Check with `events.getEventListeners(signal, 'abort')`.

questions.stem: An insurance quoting service calls a legacy SOAP backend at 3 000 rps through `new http.Agent({ keepAlive: false })`, added years ago to "avoid stale connections". At peak, p99 is dominated by TCP and TLS handshakes, the backend's CPU is pegged on new connections, and the hosts show tens of thousands of sockets in `TIME_WAIT`. Which change fits?

options.text: Give the SOAP backend more CPU so it can complete all those handshakes faster.
options.why: It pays for capacity spent on repeated handshakes; the per-request connection churn and TIME_WAIT build-up continue and grow with traffic.

options.text: A keep-alive agent with bounded `maxSockets` and a shorter idle timeout.
options.why: Reused connections remove the per-request handshake and TIME_WAIT churn; the bound protects the backend, and the shorter idle timeout avoids reusing sockets the backend has closed.

options.text: Retry failed calls with backoff.
options.why: Retries open even more short-lived connections exactly when connection setup is the bottleneck.

options.text: Add pods so each one opens fewer connections.
options.why: TIME_WAIT is per host and port tuple, so it spreads somewhat, but the per-request churn continues.

questions.explain: A new connection per request costs handshakes and leaves TIME_WAIT sockets that can exhaust ephemeral ports. Keep connections alive, bound the pool, and keep the client's idle timeout shorter than the server's to avoid stale-socket resets.

questions.stem: A Node 24 API is exposed directly through a TCP-only Network Load Balancer, with no HTTP proxy in front. A security test opens 20 000 connections that send headers one byte every 10 s. The service stops accepting new requests although CPU is idle. Which change fits best?

options.text: Raise the process file-descriptor limit to 1 million.
options.why: Slow clients then hold even more connections; you raise the ceiling without bounding the attack.

options.text: Lower `server.headersTimeout` and `server.requestTimeout` to a few seconds, or put an HTTP proxy that buffers requests in front.
options.why: Tight header and request deadlines drop slow senders quickly; a buffering proxy absorbs slow clients so Node sees only complete requests.

options.text: Lower `keepAliveTimeout` to 1 s.
options.why: That timer applies between requests on an idle connection, not while headers are still arriving.

options.text: Scale out pods until the connections fit.
options.why: An attacker's slow connections cost them almost nothing, so they can scale faster than your pods.

questions.explain: Each phase of a connection needs its own deadline: headers, the whole request, idle keep-alive. Exposing Node directly means you own slowloris protection; usually a buffering proxy or load balancer does it for you.

questions.stem: A Node API's shutdown is shown. Clients use keep-alive. On SIGTERM, in-flight requests finish, but the process takes up to 5 seconds longer than expected to exit, and sometimes gets SIGKILLed during busy rollouts. Which change fixes it without dropping in-flight requests?

options.text: Call `server.closeAllConnections()` right after `server.close()`.
options.why: It exits fast but also cuts in-flight requests, which is what the drain is meant to prevent.

options.text: Set `server.keepAliveTimeout = 0` at start-up.
options.why: It disables keep-alive for all traffic, adding connection churn in normal operation to fix shutdown.

options.text: After SIGTERM, answer with `Connection: close`, call `server.closeIdleConnections()` as responses finish, and keep a hard-deadline fallback.
options.why: `server.close()` closes only connections idle at that moment; busy keep-alive sockets stay open until `keepAliveTimeout`. Closing each one as it goes idle, with an unref'd deadline, drains quickly and safely.

options.text: Replace `process.exit(0)` with `process.exitCode = 0`.
options.why: That only changes how the exit happens; the process still waits for the open keep-alive sockets.

questions.explain: `server.close()` stops listening and closes idle connections, but connections that were busy at that moment stay open as keep-alive afterwards. A complete drain closes them as they go idle, and a hard deadline backs everything up.

questions.stem: A document-upload API accepts uploads that take up to 60 s on mobile networks. Pods drain correctly on SIGTERM, but `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is the default 30. Each deploy, support receives complaints about failed uploads. Which change fixes it?

options.text: Raise the grace period above the longest request plus drain time, e.g. 90 s.
options.why: Kubernetes sends SIGKILL when the grace period ends; it must cover the longest legitimate in-flight request plus time for endpoint removal.

options.text: Ask the mobile clients to retry any upload that fails during a deploy window.
options.why: Retries recover some uploads but waste mobile users' data and time on every deploy.

options.text: Use resumable chunked uploads only for files over 1 GB.
options.why: Resumable uploads are a good pattern, but the 60 s uploads that fail are mostly smaller than that.

options.text: Deploy only at night when there are fewer uploads.
options.why: It reduces the damage but leaves failed uploads at every deploy and slows delivery.

questions.explain: A graceful drain only works if the platform waits for it. The termination grace period must exceed the longest request you promise to finish; for very long transfers, make them resumable so a cut costs little.

questions.stem: A team added OpenTelemetry to an ESM Node 24 service by importing `./tracing.mjs` as the first line of `server.mjs`. HTTP server spans appear, but there are no spans for Postgres or outbound HTTP, so traces stop at the service boundary. Which change fixes it?

options.text: Increase the trace sampling rate to 100%.
options.why: Sampling decides which traces are kept; it can't create spans for libraries that were never instrumented.

options.text: Add manual spans around every database and outbound HTTP call in the code.
options.why: It works, but it is a lot of code to maintain and misses calls inside libraries.

options.text: Register OTel's ESM loader hook and preload `tracing.mjs` with `node --import`.
options.why: ESM bindings can't be patched after load, so OTel wraps modules through its loader hook `@opentelemetry/instrumentation/hook.mjs` (OTel documents `--experimental-loader=…`; `module.register` still works but is doc-deprecated since Node 24.15); `--import` runs the setup before any app module loads.

options.text: Switch the whole service to CommonJS and preload the tracing setup with `node --require`.
options.why: CommonJS with `--require` can work, but it rewrites the module system of the whole service to avoid a startup-order fix.

questions.explain: Auto-instrumentation must be in place before the modules it patches load. In CommonJS that is `--require ./tracing.js`; in ESM, exports are live bindings that can't be monkey-patched, so OTel needs its loader hook (`--experimental-loader=@opentelemetry/instrumentation/hook.mjs`, or `module.register`, which Node 24.15+ marks deprecated in favour of `module.registerHooks`) together with `--import ./tracing.mjs`. Missing spans for specific libraries usually mean the instrumentation came too late.

questions.stem: A booking API's p99 latency doubled after a traffic increase. Pod CPU is 30%, event-loop utilization is about 0.3, and event-loop delay p99 is 4 ms. The service uses `pg.Pool({ max: 10 })` and calls two partner APIs. Which two measurements most likely reveal the bottleneck? (Choose two.)

options.text: Time spent waiting to acquire a pool connection, with `pool.waitingCount`
options.why: With an idle loop and CPU, requests are probably waiting somewhere; a saturated pool shows up as acquire wait and a growing `waitingCount`.

options.text: Per-dependency latency histograms for the two partner calls, from traces or metrics
options.why: If a partner slowed down, its share of request time grows; per-dependency timing shows that directly.

options.text: A heap snapshot of one pod
options.why: Memory isn't implicated by any signal here, and a snapshot pauses the pod.

options.text: A CPU profile with `--cpu-prof`
options.why: With ELU at 0.3 and low loop delay, CPU isn't the constraint; a profile will show mostly idle time.

options.text: The total request rate per pod
options.why: You already know traffic rose; the rate doesn't say where the time goes.

questions.explain: When latency rises while the loop and CPU are idle, the time is spent waiting: on a pool, a lock or a dependency. Instrument the waits (pool acquire time, per-dependency latency) rather than profiling CPU.
